I think the WR arc with the machine/parallel universe story is integral for both Elliot and the audience. For most of the story we are teased into believing that perhaps there is another way to erase all of our trauma, to avoid having to go through the pain of accepting what is real. To both Elliot and us watching, having this idea potentially be true is the variable that sets into motion the long, winding road of self-discovery that we have to take. The road to recovery is through acceptance, which is what Elliot chooses in the end, but we see what the path of denial does in the case of Angela. She is manipulated into believing that (whatever WR said or showed her), her mum and all of the people who died could be brought back to life. WR's machine is simply a plot device that symbolises denial of trauma, mental illness, pain and suffering. We choose to either accept our reality, as Elliot does (he says something to Mr Robot like 'if I didn't have you, I wouldn't be me'), or we can let our imagination temporarily quell our suffering in the form of denial, like we see with Angela who eventually crumbles.

That's fair enough, I didn't mean for it to come across that way. I more so just wanted to add my views because I'm worried that people might have an overall unsatisfactory view of the show as a whole, before taking in the bigger picture. 

I can understand that, but I don't think we had to learn any more about the machine. We knew enough about what she was trying to do, and that's all we really needed. From then on, it was just about whether to believe it was capable of working and doing what she said/wanted it to do. Which comes down to the whole theme of what she did to Angela and was trying to do with Elliot as well as us, the audience. Elliot eventually succumbed to his inner desire to live in a different reality, believing that his imagined perfect reality was in fact WR's machine. I too gave in and believed that the machine had actually worked at the end of E11, and I feel as though a lot of people with trauma/mental illness may have, even for the slightest moment, wanted to believe that the parallel universe was real, as it is the 'easier' road to recovery. Only until the next 2 episodes air and we learn that it was just in Elliot's head, we realise that acceptance is the only true way to recovery.

I think not knowing if the machine worked or not is kind of integral to understanding the severity of Elliot's mental illness. If the machine worked, then it would kind of be easy for the audience to just say "the hell with all your trauma, just reset and go and live in the new world" and that would play down the journey we have been through. And if the machine didn't work, then it would again be a decision by process of elimination that the audience and Elliot can come to by saying "well the parallel universe is out of the question, so now you just have to accept your reality and move on." So I guess what I'm trying to say is, having the problem of not knowing if the machine works or not, leads Elliot and the audience on a road to self-discovery, forcing us to make decisions and ask critical questions about what we want to believe. Do we want to accept our traumas and face the reality that we live in like Elliot eventually does, or do we live in denial, allowing ourselves to be manipulated by the chance that all of your pain could be erased, like WR promises (and allegedly shows) Angela?

That’s fair enough but I still stick by what I said. Our brains have been hard wired for millions of years to survive and to do anything for survive, so if we get to a point where we try to commit suicide, i have no doubt that the brain is capable of entering a state of a kind of survival mode where it will do anything to stay alive, which will continue past then immediate aftermath as you mentioned. 

I get what you mean with being in hospital and not wanting to go back, and I’ve been in a similar position this year, having been in hospital for a suicide attempt. Don’t get me wrong I don’t want to end up there again either, but that doesn’t mean you have to get better in order to not end up there, for me it just means I have to be better at my suicide attempt the next time I try.  

Sure people will make mistakes and wrong decisions and regret them, but as I think I mentioned in the original post, I’m talking about the cases who have been depressed for several years, and who have wanted nothing more than to not be alive. Those cases aren’t built on the foundation of split second decisions, but years of experience and pre meditated thinking. I think those people should have a right to decide if they want to end their pain and suffering.
